content_selection.rationale: The brief's core picks are strong and well-supported: Anthropic's report on unintended model actions, the White House saying incident disclosure is "not optional", OpenAI's grader-sabotage report, the OpenAI revenue correction, Broadcom's chip financing, Nvidia–Reflection and the follow-up on OpenAI's math papers. Leaving out stories from before the coverage window (DeepSeek's round, Finland's order against Google, Meta Muse) and single-source items that couldn't be verified (StepFun, Reka, Aaronson) was the right call. The clearest miss is Satya Nadella's October 10 essay arguing that all AI models should be assumed compromised. TechCrunch, The Verge and others covered it widely, it fell inside the window, and it fits the brief's own lead theme of incident disclosure. Anthropic's October 8 usage policy rewrite was also widely covered and was dropped without a clear reason. A few low-weight headline-only items (Cloudflare–Deno, the Manus raise) are marginal but harmless.
content_selection.evidence: The brief's lead theme is "Labs' own misbehavior disclosures collided with Washington," yet the candidate list shows "[excluded] Nadella 'assume AI models are compromised' post (Oct 10) (explainx (second-hand; primary post not read))".

selection_disagreements.story: Nadella 'assume AI models are compromised' / 'emergency brake' post (Oct 10)
selection_disagreements.rationale: Searching showed this was not a thin second-hand item. TechCrunch ran it as 'Microsoft's Satya Nadella says AI models need an emergency brake' on Oct 10, The Verge and Benzinga also covered it, and Nadella posted it on X and his blog. He calls for treating models as insider risks, assuming they are compromised, keeping tamper-proof audit trails and having a pause/kill switch, and he explicitly backs incident reporting. TechCrunch tied it to the growing number of labs acknowledging loss-of-control incidents, which makes it a natural fit next to the Anthropic, OpenAI and White House stories the brief led with. The primary source was easy to find, so the reason given for exclusion doesn't hold.

Anthropic published it on Oct 8, inside the brief's Oct 7–10 window, and it drew broad coverage: The Verge, MacRumors, Quartz, Unite.ai and Notebookcheck. It is Anthropic's first usage policy update in over a year. It bans sustained abuse of Claude and tightens rules on weapons software, surveillance and deceptive influence campaigns. It also drops the blanket ban on personalized political targeting and adds a requirement that operators can halt Claude when it controls physical hardware. That deserved at least a headline line, especially in an issue so focused on Anthropic's safety and governance.

factual_accuracy.rationale: I checked most of the brief's main claims against primary or near-primary sources, and they hold up. That covers Anthropic's report and the White House 'not optional' statement, the FT's '$50B' OpenAI revenue figure, the FT/Reuters report on Nvidia and Reflection, the 3 withdrawn and 14 revised OpenAI math papers, OpenAI's grader misalignment report, the Memento 3 abstract, Microsoft Decision-1's price and benchmark table, Epoch's InnovationEval figures and the Gemini agent details. One real error is in the Broadcom section: the 'Broadcom shares fell about 6%' and BofA $370B figures come from an August 2026 Benzinga piece, but the brief folds them into this week's financing story as if they were current. There are also small mismatches. The FT gave Reflection's $25B valuation as a March round, not 'as of April'. 'Nexus' is OpenAI's chip program, not the chip's name. One source puts Oracle's drop at 4.9%, not 'more than 5%'. Several headline-only items (the Senate report, the Berkeley study, Apple's iPhone 18 cuts, the Manus raise) were not checked.
factual_accuracy.evidence: Brief: 'BofA estimated such financing vehicles could carry up to $370B of senior debt by mid-2029; Broadcom shares fell about 6%.' Benzinga's linked related story about that 6% drop is dated August 2026 (URL path 26/08), not October.

length_format.rationale: The brief has 14 Headlines bullets, inside the 8-15 range, and 10 deep-dives across all five tiered sections (2/3/2/1/2), the top of the 5-10 range; no empty sections are shown. The structure fully matches the template: one-line summary, Headlines, tiered sections, and sourced deep-dives. The one deviation is length: nearly every deep-dive runs to the 6-sentence maximum with very long, semicolon-chained sentences, and at least two (Decision-1 and InnovationEval) reach about 7 sentences. That is mild overshoot rather than serious bloat.
length_format.evidence: The Decision-1 deep-dive runs about 7 sentences, ending with 'Separately, Liquid AI released open-weight d1-3B and d1-omni-600M decision models...' before its 'Why it matters' line. The Anthropic item packs four incident categories, a timing dispute and the White House response into roughly 6 very long sentences.

dedup.rationale: Every story in today's brief that overlaps a prior edition is explicitly labelled as a follow-up, in both the headline and the section title, and each adds substantial new reporting. The repeats are the OpenAI math release, the Broadcom/Oracle/SpaceX chip-debt story, the decision-model race and Reflection/Beam. The remaining stories have no counterpart in the Oct 7–9 briefs: Anthropic's unintended-actions report and White House response, OpenAI's revenue correction, the OpenAI grader misalignment report, Gemini agent, Memento 3, InnovationEval, and the Senate, Berkeley, Apple and Manus/Deno headlines. Background recaps, such as the 722-manuscript count and Beam specs, are brief and explicitly framed as context.
